claims.text: What the strip looks like Diffuse, concave-up ST elevation that is not confined to one vascular territory.
claims.quote: Diffuse concave-up ST elevation (not confined to a vascular territory)

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) ST segment: diffuse concave-up elevation, not confined to a vascular territory
claims.quote: Diffuse concave-up ST elevation (not confined to a vascular territory)

claims.text: How much: ST elevation is typically modest (0.5–1 mm), measured against the T-P segment baseline
claims.quote: NB. ST- and PR-segment changes are relative to the baseline formed by the T-P segment. The degree of ST elevation is typically modest (0.5 – 1mm).

claims.text: PR segment: depression (especially in II); PR elevation in aVR
claims.quote: PR depression (especially in II; PR elevation in aVR)

claims.text: Reciprocal changes: typically no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR/V1)
claims.quote: Typically no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR/V1)

claims.text: Q waves: no pathologic Q waves
claims.quote: Unlike myocardial infarction, acute pericarditis does not cause reciprocal depression in ST segments (except in leads aVR and V1), and there are no pathologic Q waves.

claims.text: Rate: sinus tachycardia is also common (pain and/or effusion)
claims.quote: Sinus tachycardia is also common in acute pericarditis due to pain and/or pericardial effusion

claims.text: Evolution: evolves through four (Spodick) stages
claims.quote: Evolves through four Spodick stages

claims.text: Stages: 1 — widespread ST elevation and PR depression, reciprocal changes in aVR (first two weeks); 2 — ST changes normalize, T waves flatten (1 to 3 weeks); 3 — flattened T waves invert (3 to several weeks); 4 — ECG returns to normal (several weeks onwards)
claims.quote: Stage 1 – widespread STE and PR depression with reciprocal changes in aVR (occurs during the first two weeks) Stage 2 – normalisation of ST changes; generalised T wave flattening (1 to 3 weeks) Stage 3 – flattened T waves become inverted (3 to several weeks) Stage 4 – ECG returns to normal (several weeks onwards)

claims.text: Less than 50% of patients go through all four stages, and the changes may not follow this pattern
claims.quote: NB. Less than 50% of patients progress through all four classical stages and evolution of changes may not follow this typical pattern.

claims.text: Stage 3 vs ischemia: the T waves invert after the ST segment has returned to baseline, unlike acute ischemia or MI
claims.quote: Stage 3: T waves are inverted throughout the ECG; T wave–inversion occurs after the ST segment has returned to baseline and thus differs from the pattern of acute ischemia or MI.

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: the widespread ST changes come from involvement of the underlying epicardium (myopericarditis)
claims.quote: Widespread ST segment changes occur due to involvement of the underlying epicardium (i.e. myopericarditis)

claims.text: Infectious pericarditis is most often viral or idiopathic (often presumed viral) in North America and Western Europe; tuberculosis is the most common cause where it is endemic
claims.quote: Infectious pericarditis is most often viral or idiopathic (often presumed to be viral) in North America and Western Europe (1). Tuberculosis, on the other hand, is the most common cause in regions where it is endemic.

claims.text: Causes: infectious (mainly viral, e.g., coxsackie; occasionally bacterial, fungal, TB), immunologic (SLE, rheumatic fever), uremia, post-MI or after cardiac surgery (Dressler syndrome), trauma, paraneoplastic, drugs (e.g., isoniazid, cyclosporine), post-radiotherapy
claims.quote: Infectious – mainly viral (e.g. coxsackie virus); occasionally bacterial, fungal, TB. Immunological – SLE, rheumatic fever Uraemia Post-myocardial infarction or following cardiac surgery (Dressler’s syndrome) Trauma Paraneoplastic syndromes Drug-induced (e.g. isoniazid, cyclosporin) Post-radiotherapy

claims.text: Symptoms Classic: pleuritic chest pain, fever, and a pericardial rub, sometimes dyspnea
claims.quote: The classic symptoms and signs of acute pericarditis are pleuritic chest pain, fever, and a pericardial rub, and sometimes dyspnea.

claims.text: Chest pain is often retrosternal, pleuritic and positional (relieved by sitting forward, worse lying flat)
claims.quote: Chest pain is often retrosternal in nature, pleuritic, and positional (relieved by sitting forward, worse lying flat)

claims.text: The most important physical finding is a triphasic (or systolic and diastolic) precordial friction rub — often intermittent and evanescent
claims.quote: The most important physical finding is a triphasic or a systolic and diastolic precordial friction rub. However, the rub is often intermittent and evanescent

claims.text: The first evidence can be tamponade: hypotension, shock, or pulmonary edema
claims.quote: The first evidence can be tamponade, with hypotension, shock, or pulmonary edema

claims.text: Treatment First line (uncomplicated): aspirin 325 to 650 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours or another NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen 600 to 800 mg every 6 to 8 hours), usually with colchicine (e.g., 0.5 or 0.6 mg once or twice daily)
claims.quote: First-line therapy for uncomplicated pericarditis is aspirin (325 to 650 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours) or another NSAID (eg, ibuprofen 600 to 800 mg orally every 6 to 8 hours), usually in combination with colchicine (eg, 0.5 or 0.6 mg once or twice daily)

claims.text: Consider a proton pump inhibitor for NSAID gastric tolerability
claims.quote: A proton pump inhibitor should be considered to improve the gastric tolerability of NSAIDs.

claims.text: Temporary exercise restriction; interleukin-1 inhibitors or glucocorticoids may be added for selected patients when the cause is noninfectious
claims.quote: Inflammation is treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and/or colchicine and temporary exercise restriction; interleukin-1 inhibitors or glucocorticoids may be added for selected patients in whom the cause is noninfectious.

claims.text: Hospitalize some patients: especially moderate or large effusions or high-risk features (fever, subacute onset, immunosuppression, recent trauma, oral anticoagulants, no response to aspirin/NSAIDs, myopericarditis)
claims.quote: Hospitalization is warranted for some patients with an initial episode of acute pericarditis, particularly those with moderate or large effusions or with high-risk features, such as elevated temperature, subacute onset, immunosuppression, recent trauma, oral anticoagulant therapy, failure to respond to an initial course of aspirin or NSAIDs, and myopericarditis.

claims.text: Early echo (TTE) looks for complications such as a large effusion and tamponade
claims.quote: TTE is useful in the early assessment of patients with suspected pericarditis to look for complications such as large pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade
